lines.text: Your body does weird stuff every single day!
It hiccups, it yawns, it sneezes at the sun,
and sometimes it jolts you awake, just as you fall asleep.
So here are ten weird things your body does, and the real reason behind each one.
Some of them, even scientists are still arguing about!
Number one: hiccups!
Under your lungs sits a big, dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm.
With every normal breath, it pulls down smoothly, and air flows in.
But when the nerves that control it get irritated,
say from eating too fast, fizzy drinks, or a sudden change in temperature,
the diaphragm suddenly spasms, and yanks air in!
A split second later, your vocal cords snap shut,
and that sudden stop is the hic you hear!
Most hiccups go away on their own, within minutes.
But one man, Charles Osborne, hiccupped for sixty-eight years, from nineteen twenty-two to nineteen ninety!
It's a world record nobody wants.
And here's the strange part: scientists still aren't sure why we have them at all.
Number two: yawning.
You've probably heard that you yawn because you need more oxygen.
But studies haven't found a link between yawning and the oxygen in your blood.
One leading idea is that a yawn cools your brain,
pulling in a big gulp of air, and pumping blood toward your head, like a radiator.
In one study, people yawned more in cooler weather than in hot weather,
And that makes sense, because cooler air cools better.
And yes, yawns really are contagious.
You might even yawn just hearing about it, right now.
Number three: sneezing at the sun!
Step out into bright light, and some people instantly sneeze.
It's called the photic sneeze reflex,
and estimates say somewhere between eighteen and thirty-five percent of people have it.
It often runs in families.
The best guess is that the nerve signals from your eyes and your nose run very close together,
so a blast of light gets mixed up with an itch in your nose.
Nobody has proven exactly how it works yet.
Number four: brain freeze.
You take a big bite of ice cream, and boom! A sudden pain in your forehead.
The cold hits the roof of your mouth,
where there's a bundle of nerves called the sphenopalatine ganglion.
Doctors even call it sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia. Try saying that fast!
One theory is that the blood vessels there react to the sudden cold,
and your brain reads it as pain in your head.
The fix? Press your tongue on the roof of your mouth, to warm it up,
or just eat cold stuff slowly.
It hurts, but it's harmless, and it passes in seconds.
Number five: the hypnic jerk.
You're drifting off to sleep, and suddenly it feels like you're falling,
and your whole body jolts you awake!
That's a hypnic jerk, also called a sleep start.
Up to seventy percent of people get them.
Nobody knows for sure why they happen.
One idea is that as your muscles relax, your brain is switching from awake to asleep,
and that switch can misfire into a quick twitch.
Caffeine, stress, and being very tired can make them more likely.
They're harmless. Just a little rude.
Number six: goosebumps.
Get cold, or hear an amazing song, and tiny bumps pop up all over your skin.
Each one is a tiny muscle, pulling a hair straight up.
Doctors call them cutis anserina, which literally means goose skin.
For furry animals, that makes their fur stand up and trap warm air,
or makes them look bigger, to scare off a threat.
We lost most of our fur, but we kept the reflex.
So goosebumps are just a leftover, from our hairy ancestors!
Number seven: wrinkly fingers in the bath.
Most people think your skin just soaks up water and puckers.
But here's the twist: it's actually your nerves doing it!
Your nervous system shrinks the blood vessels in your fingertips,
and the skin on top folds into wrinkles.
In fact, if the nerve to a finger is damaged, that finger doesn't wrinkle at all!
One idea is that wrinkles work like tire treads, helping you grip wet things.
In one study, people with wrinkly fingers moved wet marbles about twelve percent faster,
but a later study found no difference, so the jury's still out.
Number eight: cracking your knuckles.
That pop is not your bones grinding.
Your joints sit in a slippery fluid,
and when you pull the joint apart, a gas-filled bubble forms in that fluid, with a pop!
Scientists actually filmed it happening inside an MRI scanner, in twenty fifteen.
So, will it give you arthritis?
One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand, for sixty years.
Neither hand got arthritis.
He even won an Ig Nobel prize for it, in two thousand nine!
And bigger studies haven't found a link either.
Number nine: your stomach growling.
That rumble isn't your stomach begging for food.
It's gas and liquid being squeezed through your gut by waves of muscle.
A couple of hours after your stomach empties, a cleaning wave sweeps the leftovers along,
and with no food inside to muffle it, the sound gets loud!
Your gut rumbles when you're full too; the food just muffles it.
Doctors even have a name for it: borborygmi.
And number ten: your foot falling asleep.
Most people think the blood gets cut off.
But mostly, you're squashing a nerve.
The squashed nerve stops carrying messages, so your foot goes numb.
When you move, the pressure comes off, and the nerve fires a messy burst of signals,
which your brain reads as pins and needles!
So your body isn't broken. It's just running some very old, very weird code!
Which one surprised you most? Tell me in the comments,
and subscribe to solo hype, for a weird true fact every day!
